caseno: Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 with Civil Revision No, 1058 of 2001.
lawyer:
Minal Kanti Biswas, Advocate-For the Petitioner. 
Gobinda Chandra Tagore, Advocate-For the Opposite Party
parties:
Swapon Kumar Gain ------ Petitioner
Vs.   
Amita Golder ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
7. Mr Gobinda Chandra Tagore, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, supports the decision of the lower appellate Court and submits that the defendant did not appear in the suit to contest the suit and did not file any written statement and thereby admitted the assertions made by the plaintiff in the plaint and thus on the admission of the defendant the suit could be decreed. The learned Advocate has further submitted that, the Court of the District Judge is the principal civil Court of the District and an appeal lies from a judgment, decree or Order of a Family Court to the District Judge who is not a persona designata and the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure for additional evidence is applicable. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Moinuddin (Md) vs Amina Khan Majlish reported in 42 DLR 483 in support of his submission that under section 17 (1) of the Family Court Ordinance an appeal shall lie from a judgment, decree or order of Family Court to "the Court of the District Judge" The latter being a civil Court, provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure applies in the appeal preferred before the learned District Judge who is not a persona designata but a civil Court. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Md Sirajul Islam vs Helana Begum and others reported in 3 BLT 40. The learned Advocate has further relied on a decision in the case of Hasibur Rahman (Md) vs Shakila Begum and others reported in 53 DLR 152 in support of his submission that the District Judge referred to in section 17(1) of the Family Court Ordinance is the Judge of the principal Civil Court of the District and never a persona designata and the Code of Civil Procedure is very much applicable to family appellate proceeding before the learned District Judge. The learned Advocate further relied on a decision in the case of Utpal Kanti Das vs Monju Rani Das reported in 50 DLR (AD) 47 to support his submission that, once the celebration of a marriage in fact is established there shall be a presumption of there being a marriage in law and observance of the essential ceremonies. 

 8. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and all other evidence on record. It is not disputed that the suit was decreed ex parte and the defendant challenged the ex parte decree by filing a case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and got the ex parte decree set aside and the suit was restored but did not appear to contest the suit by filing any written statement. The plaint shows that the plaintiff clearly made an assertion that marriage under the Hindu law in terms of Vedic ceremonies was observed in Dhakeswari Mandir by a Purohit this clear assertion of the plaintiff, as made in the plaint, has not been denied or challenged by the defendant by filing any written statement. The plaintiff, however, made an assertion that there was exchange of garlands before the deity Kalimatha but such statement alone would not disqualify the marriage held in  Dhakeswari Mandir by a "Purohit" upon observance of all formalities as required under the Hindu Law. The lower appellate Court being the final Court of fact has, on consideration of the evidence on record, come to a finding of fact that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. This finding of fact with regard to marriage carried a valid presumption that a marriage in law under the Hindu system was solemnised upon observance of all the legal formalities including saptapadi and invocation before the sacred fire. I have myself perused the plaint and the evidence of 'Purohit' who solemnised the marriage and stated in his evidence that there was saptapadi at the time of marriage also. The defendant has not taken any step to dislodge the evidence touching observance of essential ceremonies of marriage under the Hindu Law. When a marriage, in fact, is proved our Appellate Division in 50 DLR (AD) 47 held "As marriages in fact has been proved in this case, marriage in law must be presumed. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, it is, therefore, amply proved that the plaintiff and the defendant were married according to the Hindu Shastra" Admittedly, the defendant did not raise the plea of invalidity of the marriage because of non-performance of any essential ceremony. In view of the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division, we are permitted to presume a valid marriage in law from the finding of fact of the appellate Court that a marriage, in fact, took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. I have already noticed that the defendant did not deny or challenge the factum of marriage between the plaintiff and the defendant. I am therefore, inclined to take the view, in agreement with the learned District Judge, that a legal and valid marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant upon observance of all legal formalities according to Hindu Shastra. 

 9. I am now called upon to consider whether additional evidence is permissible before the appellate Court against a judgment, decree or order passed by the Family Court. An appeal lies to the learned District Judge against a judgment, decree and order of Family Court under section 17(1) of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. The Court of the District Judge has not been defined in the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. I am therefore, in respectful agreement with the view expressed by a single Bench in the case reported in 53 DLR 152 holding "District Judge" means the "Judge of the Principal Civil Court" of the District. The "District Judge" as the 'Family Appellate Judge' cannot be ascribed to be 'Persona Designata' 'District Judge' being the "Principal Judge of the Civil Court" of the District, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure is very much applicable to family appellate proceeding before Judge or the transferee Judges like Additional District Judge and Subordinate Judge. "The same view was expressed by a Division Bench in the case reported in 42 DLR 483 holding the view that "Thus there is no scope for thinking that the District Judge referred to in the said Ordinance is a persona designata or a Family Court; On the other hand, it appears that the appellate Court under the said Ordinance also includes any Court of Additional District Judge or Subordinate Judge under the administrative control of the District Judge. These are all Civil Courts and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to proceeding before these Courts", The decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 172 relates to the provision of Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 and their Lordships of the Appellate Division took the view that the District Judge mentioned in the said Ordinance is not a persona designata but is a Principal Civil Court of the District and is subject to both the appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division, From the aforesaid decisions it is concluded that a Family Appellate Court is a Court permitted to receive additional evidence under Order XLI, 1 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned District Judge has taken additional evidence in respect of both documentary and oral evidence and, on consideration of those documents, came to the conclusion that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. This finding of fact of the final Court of fact being based on assessment and consideration of evidence, I do not find any ground to disagree with such finding of fact. The learned Advocate for the petitioner could not point out any misreading of evidence or non-consideration of evidence or misconstruction of evidence to permit this revisional Court to disturb the finding of fact recorded by the final Court of fact. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the memorandum of appeal before the learned District Judge filed by the plaintiff- appellant was not signed by the plaintiff-appellant is totally incorrect and misconceived, I have myself perused the memorandum of appeal preferred before the learned District Judge, Dhaka and I find that on all the pages of the memorandum of appeal the plaintiff-appellant had put her signature. The memorandum of appeal before the appellate Court contains 4 pages and in all the 4 pages I find the signature of the plaintiff-appellant. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that two essential ceremonies, such as, saptapadi and invocation before sacred fire of a valid marriage under the Hindu law have not been proved by the plaintiff is again without any basis. The evidence on record, clearly indicate that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant in Dhakeswari Mandir conducted by a "Purohit" and the said "Purohit" in his evidence stated that he conducted the marriage upon compliance of all the formalities of Hindu Shastra. The evidence of the "Purohit" was corroborated by 4 other witnesses who were present during marriage in Dhakeswari Mandir. The decision reported in 35 DLR 160 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner though arises out of a Criminal Proceeding is of no help to the learned Advocate as a valid presumption is permitted to be drawn from the fact that marriage between the plaintiff and the defendant took place in Dhakeswari Mandir. The presumption is that all the legal formalities under the Hindu law were complied with and though such presumption is rebuttable but the defendant has not rebutted the presumption. I have already held that the plaintiff has proved a valid marriage under the Hindu law between the plaintiff and the defendant. The decision reported in, 2 BLC 509 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner relates to a marriage under the Muslim law and has no manner of application in respect of marriage under the Hindu law. The decision reported in 34 DLR 221 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner also relates to Muslim marriage and can not be applied in connection with Hindu marriage. In view of my above consideration, I do not find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner' in Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000.
